description: I’m a software engineer with prior experience in hackathons and startups. I’m looking for teammates who enjoy solving problems, sharing ideas, and building together. Prior hackathon experience or experience working on software teams is prefered but not required.
summary:
SkyDive is a web tool that turns any patch of sky into a movie covering sixteen years. Enter coordinates and it lines up WISE images from 2010 to 2024, Pan-STARRS epochs, and SPHEREx visits from 2025 onward in 102 infrared colours. You can play a video that iterates through frames, stack and subtract groups of visits so anything that moved or changed stands out, click a source to get its spectrum and light curve, and overlay Gaia, CatWISE, asteroid and variable-star catalogues, with each marker moved to the frame's date. A 3D map holds 331,802 stars and brown dwarfs within 100 parsecs, with a ±50,000-year time slider; click a star to open its SPHEREx view.

A single SPHEREx pixel is 6.2″ across, so on its own SPHEREx cannot show slow motion. Adding the WISE frames stretches the baseline to sixteen years, and that makes the motion visible. Barnard's Star, for example, moves about 145″ across the WISE frames. The browser holds every aligned exposure, so stacking, choosing wavelengths and measuring spectra happen instantly, and anyone with a browser can search for moving or changing objects without downloading archive files or writing code.
details:
What it does: Enter sky coordinates and SkyDive plays a movie of that patch of sky from 2010 to today. The movie joins WISE images (2010–2024), Pan-STARRS images and SPHEREx images (2025 onward, 102 infrared colours). You can flick between dates, or subtract one date from another so anything that moved stands out. Clicking an object shows its spectrum and how its brightness changes over time. A 3D map shows every known star within 100 parsecs; click a star and it opens in the viewer.

How it works: A Python backend downloads only the small patch of each SPHEREx image it needs from NASA's archive, then lines all the images up. The browser gets every image, so changing colours, stacking and measuring respond instantly.

Benefits and impact: SPHEREx on its own can't show slow-moving objects, because they shift only a pixel or two during its mission. Adding the WISE images gives sixteen years of history making it possible to view slow moving objects. Students and amateur astronomers can use it to hunt for nearby brown dwarfs and moving objects without installing anything or writing code. When NASA releases new SPHEREx data, SkyDive picks it up with no code changes.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, astropy and numpy for the backend; TypeScript, Vite, three.js, uPlot and Aladin Lite for the frontend; hosting on Vercel. The data comes from NASA SPHEREx, WISE, Gaia, Hipparcos, Pan-STARRS and the Canadian Space Agency's NEOSSat.

Whats's creative: SkyDive puts four surveys on one timeline: WISE, Pan-STARRS and SPHEREx images, with Gaia star positions moved to each frame's date. Each frame shows its catalogue markers where those objects were on that date, so you can watch a star and its marker move together. The 3D map works as a way into the data, so you can fly through the stars near the Sun, pick one and land on its SPHEREx images. Every setting is saved in the URL, so a link brings back the exact view, and adding embed=1 lets you put the viewer on another web page. Because the browser holds every image, picking colours, stacking dates and clicking for a spectrum all happen with no waiting.

What we considered: We built SkyDive iteratively, continously improving it after each feature was added. The first frontend worked but was hard to read and use, it had 102 toggles for each wavelength of light, so we redesigned it: a live 3D map on the home page, clearer type and plain labels, then fixes to zooming and loading speed, then adding in the slider for filtering wavelengths. On the backend we started with SPHEREx alone and kept adding sources as we went: WISE for the long history, Pan-STARRS (pulling in neighbouring sky tiles to fill gaps), Gaia and CatWISE markers, asteroids, variable stars and NEOSSat. Each new source exposed problems in the interface, which sent us back to the frontend again.
